About this citation

The Analects is a compiled record of sayings, not a work by Confucius. The common formula 'Confucius said' refers to a tradent whose words were assembled by later hands, and the book-and-chapter locator is what makes a passage findable in any edition.

Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“The Master said: You, shall I teach you what knowing is? To know what you know, and to know what you do not know — that is true knowing.”
Classical Chinese
“知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也。”

Four clauses built on one repeated character, 知 (to know). The English has to alternate between “know” and “do not know” to reproduce a chiasmus Chinese produces by repetition.

Attribution notes

Analects 2.17, addressed to Zilu. The structure is a definition by contrast: knowing is knowing when you know and knowing when you do not. It is often filed beside the Socratic profession of ignorance, but the move is different — Confucius is defining knowledge by accuracy about its own limits, not claiming to possess none.

About Confucius

Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE) taught in the late Spring and Autumn period amid the Zhou order’s political fragmentation. Born in the state of Lu, he briefly held local office and then spent years seeking rulers who would adopt ritual-based, virtue-centered government.

How to read this passage

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge, humility.
